A foreign-currency refund can return different dollars: chart the rate and the fees

Use a cash-flow bridge, posted-amount comparisons, checkout quotes and a refund matrix to separate the foreign price from CAD conversion and fee effects.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 5 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Follow foreign purchase amounts, conversion costs and a later refund

Interactive planning lab

CAD charged on purchase$1,383.75
CAD credited on the selected refund$1,300
Net CAD cash paid after the refund$83.75

Hypothetical conversion references, fees and refund treatment; no live exchange rate or issuer policy is supplied. CAD per foreign currency unit (FCU) is multiplied by the foreign amount. Purchase cost is added to its reference CAD amount; a selected refund deduction is subtracted from its reference CAD credit. Any original-fee rebate is a separate proportional credit. These are scenario assumptions, not network settlement calculations. Partial refunds leave part of the purchase unreturned.

The central idea

Refunding the same foreign amount does not necessarily reverse the original CAD cash flow. The later conversion and the treatment of fees both matter.

01

Start with the direction of the exchange-rate quote

The original price is expressed in foreign currency units, abbreviated FCU. The reference quote is Canadian dollars per one FCU. To translate the foreign amount into reference CAD, multiply the amount by that quote. A higher CAD-per-FCU quote makes the same foreign purchase cost more Canadian dollars.

The default foreign purchase is 1,000 FCU at an assumed reference of CAD 1.35 per FCU. The reference amount is therefore CAD 1,350. A hypothetical purchase conversion cost of 2.5% adds CAD 33.75, taking the modeled charge to CAD 1,383.75.

These are chosen conversion references and separately entered costs. They are not live rates, card-network quotes or an issuer’s actual settlement formula. A price displayed on a shopping day may differ from the rate and date ultimately used under a card agreement.

02

Translate the refund independently from the purchase

The example then refunds the full 1,000 FCU at a later hypothetical reference of CAD 1.30 per FCU. That produces a CAD 1,300 reference credit. With no additional refund deduction and no original-fee rebate selected, the modeled credited amount is CAD 1,300.

Net cash paid is CAD 1,383.75 − CAD 1,300 = CAD 83.75. The difference consists of CAD 50 from the changed conversion reference and CAD 33.75 of retained purchase conversion cost. The waterfall shows each part separately.

The FCAC’s credit-card explanation describes how foreign-currency transactions and refunds can produce different Canadian-dollar amounts. The charts make that general mechanism visible with independent, editable assumptions rather than predicting the result of a particular return.

03

Treat the refund fee and an original-fee rebate as different entries

A refund can involve more than a new exchange rate. The tool has one control for a deduction from the reference refund and another for the share of the original purchase fee returned on the refunded portion. They represent different cash entries and are not automatically linked.

For example, adding a 2.5% refund deduction to the default would reduce the CAD 1,300 reference credit by CAD 32.50. Returning the full original CAD 33.75 fee would instead increase the credit by that amount. Each change should appear once in the cash-flow bridge.

Actual treatment depends on the agreement. Tangerine’s cardholder agreement provides an example with conversion charges on foreign debits and credits and a retained original conversion charge. It is a specific agreement, not a universal rule for every card. Use the current terms governing the card and transaction being reviewed.

04

Do not call the whole remaining debit a loss after a partial return

The refund-share control changes how much of the original foreign purchase is returned. At 50%, the default refund is 500 FCU. The reference credit is CAD 650, and the remaining net CAD debit is CAD 733.75 under the selected zero-refund-fee, zero-original-fee-rebate assumptions.

That net debit includes payment for the half of the purchase that was not returned. It should not be described as a CAD 733.75 exchange loss. With a full refund, the endpoint isolates the conversion and fee differences in this model; with a partial refund, retained goods or services are also part of the economic result.

An original-fee rebate is proportional to the refunded share before the selected rebate percentage is applied. If no part of the purchase is refunded, the tool generates no refund credit or fee rebate. This keeps the fee calculation aligned with the amount actually returned.

05

Compare the CAD checkout quote with the full foreign-charge cost

A merchant may offer to convert a foreign price into Canadian dollars before the charge reaches the card. Visa’s dynamic-currency-conversion guidance explains the choice and the need to inspect conversion details.

The purchase-only bar chart compares the selected foreign-charge cost with three invented CAD checkout quotes. Using the same CAD 1,350 reference, markups of 2%, 4% and 6% produce CAD 1,377, CAD 1,404 and CAD 1,431. The foreign-charge example, including its entered purchase conversion cost, is CAD 1,383.75.

The hypothetical CAD quotes assume no additional issuer charge. Actual cross-border transactions settled in CAD can have other fees, so the chart does not establish which option is cheaper on a real checkout screen. Compare all disclosed amounts and the card agreement. The chart excludes refunds, credit-card borrowing interest and any reward value.

06

Use the matrix to separate a rate change from a fee decision

The matrix sets refund references at 90%, 95%, 100% and 105% of the selected purchase reference. Its columns vary how much of the original purchase fee is returned. Purchase terms, refund share and the separately entered refund deduction stay fixed.

Read across a row to isolate the original-fee rebate. Read down a column to see the effect of the conversion reference. A negative net-cash endpoint means the modeled credit exceeds the original debit, which can happen under the entered rates. It is neither a guaranteed refund outcome nor an arbitrage strategy.

For a practical budget, keep the original statement amount, the confirmed foreign refund and the actual CAD credit. Allow for the time before the credit is usable and check the card’s payment requirements while the refund is pending. A merchant’s confirmation in foreign currency is useful evidence, but it is not the final Canadian-dollar amount in the account.

Sources and scope

Public sources reviewed on 25 October 2026. Charts labelled “Official statistics” or “Derived from official statistics” identify their source periods. Other charts are hypothetical scenarios. Original scenario calculations and research checklists are TickerLantern’s educational analysis; attributed publisher examples retain their stated source and scope. Recheck current issuer documents for any product-specific decision.

  1. FCAC · How credit cards work ↗

    Reviewed 25 October 2026 for foreign-currency charges and refund conversion context. Hypothetical conversion references and fee inputs are not reported card-network rates.

  2. Tangerine · Credit Card Cardholder Agreement ↗

    Agreement effective 22 April 2026; section 14 reviewed 25 October 2026. A specific example of foreign debit/credit conversion and original-charge treatment. Its rules are not assumed to apply to other cards; all fee controls remain independent assumptions.

  3. Visa Canada · Dynamic Currency Conversion ↗

    Reviewed 25 October 2026 for the merchant conversion choice and disclosed conversion details. The chart’s 2%, 4% and 6% markups are invented illustrations, not Visa offers or measured merchant pricing.
